claim: Due to Imran Khan's criticism of Macron's comments on Islam, French authorities cancelled the visas of 183 Pakistani citizens and deported 118 from the country.
justification: The claim originated from an impostor Twitter account (@PakConsulateFr) with only 469 followers, not the real Pakistani embassy/consulate in France. Pakistan's actual Embassy in Paris (@PakInFrance) publicly denounced the account as fake, and Pakistan's Foreign Office spokesperson explicitly called the story 'fake news' spread by 'dummy Twitter accounts.' No French government source or credible outlet independently verified any visa cancellations or deportations tied to Imran Khan's criticism of Macron.

trace.raw_text:
This claim has been thoroughly debunked as fake news that originated from an impostor Twitter account.

The multiple fact-checks are consistent: the account "@PakConsulateFr" claiming to be the "Consulate General of Pakistan France" was not authentic. The Embassy of Pakistan in Paris stressed in a notice published to clarify the issue that France has only one official account on Twitter, calling the other account fake and misleading, and urged all persons to report the fake account to avoid the spreading of fake news. Specifically, the Embassy stated "The Embassy of Pakistan in Paris, France has only one Twitter account @PakInFrance. Any other account claiming to represent the Embassy anywhere in France is fake & misleading."

Pakistan's own Foreign Office also rejected the story: FO Spokesperson Zahid Hafeez Chaudhri said, "We have noticed some fake news with regard to the Pakistani diaspora in France being spread by some sections of Indian media and dummy Twitter accounts."

Independent analysis found the impostor account had almost no credibility — the account has a mere 469 followers, none among them Pakistani government institutions or officials, which clearly indicates the account is fake. Despite this, the fake news was widely reported by Indian news organizations, including prominent platforms such as ANI, DNA, Zee News, and News18 on 1 November, which is likely how this claim spread internationally. No credible French government source, French media outlet, or verified Pakistani diplomatic account ever confirmed that France cancelled 183 visas or deported 118 Pakistanis in retaliation for Imran Khan's remarks.

justification: No UNESCO document, press release, or independent reporting confirms any such declaration; UNESCO does not issue rankings of ethnic/caste groups by antiquity, and even community-history websites making extensive claims about Nadar origins do not cite any UNESCO source. An independent fact-checking outlet (YouTurn) has a dedicated page questioning this exact claim, consistent with it being a circulating unverified/false claim.

Notably, one dedicated fact-checking organization, YouTurn (part of the People Educational Awareness Trust), a non-profit organization committed to transparent and unbiased fact-checking, has a page specifically titled "Did UNESCO has declared the Nadar community as..." — indicating this exact claim has been examined by fact-checkers as a viral/dubious claim requiring scrutiny, which is typically the pattern for debunked social-media claims.

- UNESCO, as an international body, does not issue rankings or declarations about which ethnic/caste community constitutes the "most ancient race in the world." claim: You see the number today? 33.1 GDP. The biggest in the history of our country by almost triple, right? Almost triple. Now it’s very much bigger than any GDP we’ve ever had. You have to go back to the 1950s, and then it’s less than half. This is the greatest number, 33.1 percent.
justification: The 33.1% figure and 'record' claim are accurate, but Trump's 'almost triple' comparison to the 1950s record overstates it — his own White House press release said the new record was 'nearly double' the prior one, not triple. More importantly, the claim that GDP is now 'very much bigger than any GDP we've ever had' ignores that this growth rate followed an even larger record decline (31.4%) the prior quarter, leaving the economy still smaller than its pre-pandemic level, which fact-checkers at the time flagged as the essential missing context.

trace.raw_text:
Based on the evidence, here's my assessment:

**What's accurate:** The 33.1% figure itself is correct — the US government published a report showing GDP grew at a stunning 33.1% annual rate in the third quarter of 2020, and it's true that third-quarter growth was the fastest on record in data going back to 1947. The White House itself confirmed this was a record: the economy grew 33.1% on an annualized basis in a single quarter, by far the largest in recorded history.

**What's exaggerated/misleading:**

1. **The "almost triple" comparison to the 1950s is overstated.** The White House's own press release characterized the prior record (from around 1950) as being beaten by "nearly double," not triple: real GDP grew at an annualized rate of 33.1% in the third quarter of 2020, beating expectations and setting an all-time record. This jump in GDP is nearly double the previous record set 70 years ago. "Nearly double" (roughly 33% vs ~17%) is very different from Trump's claim of "almost triple."

2. **Critical missing context:** Fact-checks at the time noted the record was mechanically produced by an even larger record collapse the prior quarter: It's impossible to ignore what happened immediately leading up to those gains: The US economy declined at a 31.4% annual rate — the deepest downturn on record. A big reason the US posted record GDP this quarter is because there was a record decline in the prior quarter. As a result, when you step back and look at that broader context, the US economy is still operating well below its pre-pandemic peak. Gross domestic product is still $670 billion lower than where it was at the end of 2019.

So while the 33.1% figure and "record" claim are technically true, Trump's framing exaggerates the magnitude of the historical comparison (claiming "almost triple" versus the actual "nearly double") and omits that this record rebound followed the largest GDP contraction on record, meaning the economy was still smaller than before the pandemic — not "very much bigger than any GDP we've ever had" as he stated.

Specifically, Weiss argued: "Mask mandates do nothing to stop [the spread of] COVID[-19]"; "The narrative simply assumes rather than proves that masks work, despite overwhelming scientific evidence to the contrary"; "The plentiful evidence we have indicates masks would not meaningfully help with aerosol transmission." 1. It misattributes to Weiss a position he did not hold — he explicitly argued masks do NOT stop COVID spread, not that they do.

claim: Even if your mail-in ballot is postmarked prior to the Election day but arrives after the Election day it will be thrown out.
justification: Fact-checkers (AllSides, The Dispatch) reviewing this exact October 2020 Facebook post found it to be an overgeneralization: while some states reject late-arriving ballots regardless of postmark, at the time 22 states plus D.C. had grace periods that counted ballots postmarked by Election Day even if they arrived afterward (e.g., Alaska allowed 10 days, California up to 17 days). Because ballot-counting rules vary by state, the blanket claim that a properly postmarked ballot 'will be thrown out' if it arrives late is false for a majority of jurisdictions.

trace.raw_text:
I found direct, well-documented fact-checking of this exact claim.

Elizabeth Gilbert's Facebook post stated that "Even if your mail-in ballot is postmarked today, if it arrives after Election Day, it will be thrown out." Fact-checkers from AllSides and The Dispatch reviewed this claim and found it to be an overgeneralization. As they explained, Gilbert's post overgeneralizes and is therefore wrong, since while it is true that some states will not count ballots that arrive after Election Day, mail-in voting deadlines vary from state to state, and many states will accept ballots that were postmarked before election day but arrive after November 3.

Specific examples cited include: Alaska, for example, will accept absentee ballots postmarked on November 3 and received 10 days after Election Day. California will accept ballots up to 17 days after the election provided they were postmarked by Election Day. Overall, 22 states plus the District of Columbia will accept ballots received some period after the election—ranging from the day after to 20 days after—provided the ballots were properly postmarked by the states' deadlines.

This is consistent with broader reporting confirming that a substantial minority of states have "grace periods" allowing postmarked ballots to count if they arrive after Election Day, though this number and the specific rules have shifted over time (some states have since eliminated these grace periods in more recent years).

So the claim, as stated in absolute terms ("even if... it will be thrown out"), is false as a general rule — it is only true in some states, not all or even most.

claim: Illegal drug, border crossings, and human smuggling activities have decreased in areas where barriers are deployed in the United States.
justification: CBP testimony to the Senate Judiciary Committee confirms a localized reduction in vehicle-based drug smuggling and shifted crossing patterns specifically in areas where barriers are built, supporting the literal claim. However, this creates a misleading overall impression because independent data show over 90% of hard drugs are seized at legal ports of entry (not barrier zones), and experts/CBP data show smugglers largely reroute to unwalled areas rather than being stopped, meaning barriers do not meaningfully reduce nationwide drug or human smuggling activity as the claim implies.

trace.raw_text:
## Assessment

The claim as literally worded — that drug smuggling, crossings, and human smuggling activity decrease specifically in the localized areas where physical barriers are built — has real support in official government testimony. claim: In the US lockdowns are partly responsible for excess deaths not directly attributed to COVID-19 which were observed in 2020.
justification: The Washington Examiner article did make this claim, but independent fact-checks (Science Feedback/Health Feedback) found it 'unsupported by scientific evidence' — the JAMA and CDC studies cited attributed non-COVID excess deaths to undocumented infections and general healthcare disruptions, not specifically to lockdowns, meaning the article extrapolated beyond what the underlying research showed.

trace.raw_text:
I have strong evidence directly addressing this claim through independent fact-checks.

The claim under review (that the Washington Examiner article by Michael Lee said lockdowns are partly responsible for excess deaths not attributed to COVID-19) is accurately quoted from the article. The article did state "One reason for the high amount of excess deaths not attributable to COVID-19 has been disruptions in health services caused by lockdowns." However, independent fact-checkers who reviewed this claim found it to be scientifically unsupported.

Health Feedback's fact-check concluded that the Washington Examiner claims that lockdowns are partly responsible for excess deaths observed in 2020 not directly attributed to COVID-19, but this claim is unsupported by scientific evidence. The fact-checkers noted that both the JAMA and CDC studies list several possible explanations for these excess deaths, notably "unrecognized or undocumented infection with severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2," and while the JAMA study also highlights "disruptions in health care access or utilization" as another possible explanation, it does not attribute disruption in healthcare access to lockdowns, as the Washington Examiner article does.

The underlying studies the article cited did not actually draw this causal link. The JAMA study's own explanation for excess deaths was framed around undocumented infections or general "disruptions in health care access," not lockdowns specifically. Science Feedback's separate review similarly concluded: it is unclear how these other excess deaths relate to the COVID-19 pandemic, and while it is possible that lockdowns may have contributed to a certain proportion of excess deaths, no data is presented in the Washington Examiner article to support the claim.

Notably, the actual data source (excess deaths not attributed to COVID-19) is also disputed in magnitude — a study posted by the CDC calculates a lower percentage of 14.5% excess deaths not caused by the virus versus the one-third figure from the JAMA study the Examiner emphasized, and the study published in JAMA had not been peer reviewed at the time.

So while it's true the Washington Examiner made this claim, and true that lockdown-related indirect harms (delayed healthcare, mental health, substance abuse) are plausible contributors discussed elsewhere, the specific causal attribution to lockdowns was not supported by the cited studies and was explicitly flagged as an evidence-free extrapolation by independent fact-checkers.

claim: Controversial abortion methods are allowed under New Zealand's Abortion Legislation Act (2020).
justification: The Act indeed does not name or restrict specific abortion techniques, which is normal for health legislation, but Right To Life UK frames this ordinary legislative silence as if it actively 'allows' extreme procedures like 'partial-birth abortion' -- a loaded, non-New Zealand legal term -- with no evidence such a specific method is used in NZ practice, where late abortions instead typically involve feticide followed by induced labour. This omits crucial context that clinical practice is still governed by professional standards, creating a misleading impression.

trace.raw_text:
Based on my research, this claim originates from Right To Life UK's own commentary on New Zealand's Abortion Legislation Act 2020, which stated there would be no legal restrictions on controversial methods of abortion such as intact dilation and extraction abortions (also known as partial-birth abortions).

Examining the actual text of the Act, it is true that the legislation does not specify or restrict particular abortion procedures/techniques. The law's provisions focus on who may provide abortion services to a woman not more than 20 weeks pregnant, and requires a health practitioner to reasonably believe the abortion is clinically appropriate for pregnancies beyond 20 weeks, without ever addressing surgical technique. So in a narrow, technical sense, it's accurate that no specific abortion method is banned by name in the statute.

However, this framing is misleading for several reasons. First, it's standard practice for health legislation not to legislate specific medical procedures/techniques by name — this is true of virtually all medical care laws, not a unique feature of this Act designed to "allow" fringe procedures. Second, the term "partial-birth abortion" (intact dilation and extraction) is a politically loaded, U.S.-specific term without a legal definition in New Zealand, and there's no evidence in the sources that this specific procedure is being performed in New Zealand — actual NZ practice for late abortions, as described by pro-life group Voice For Life, involves the abortionist usually initiating foeticide by injecting a drug into the heart to stop it, after which labour is induced and the woman goes through the delivery process, which is a different clinical approach than the procedure implied by the claim. Third, all New Zealand health practitioners remain bound by professional, ethical, and clinical standards, which the Act itself references as a requirement in assessing what is "clinically appropriate."

So while the literal statement (no explicit statutory ban on specific methods) has some basis, presenting it as "controversial methods are allowed" creates a false impression that the law specifically sanctions or has led to use of extreme procedures like "partial-birth abortion," which is not supported by evidence of actual clinical practice in New Zealand.

justification: Numerous independent fact-checks (Washington Post, USA Today/VERIFY affiliates, National Review, Federalist Society) found that while Harris was correct about the basic timeline of the 1864 Supreme Court vacancy and Lincoln's delay in nominating a replacement until after the election, she omitted the key fact that the Senate was out of session until December (making pre-election confirmation impossible regardless of intent) and that no evidence exists Lincoln ever stated the reason was to let voters decide. This claim relates to a widely fact-checked statement by Kamala Harris during the October 7, 2020 vice presidential debate, in which she claimed Abraham Lincoln declined to nominate a Supreme Court justice before the 1864 election because "the American people deserve to make the decision about who will be the next president."

Multiple independent fact-checks confirm the "missing key details" characterization. The Washington Post noted the Democratic candidate claimed in a debate with Vice President Mike Pence Wednesday night that Abraham Lincoln delayed his Supreme Court pick in 1864 so the American people could "make the decision." Multiple fact-checkers found problems with this: KING 5's VERIFY found Lincoln never said anything about letting the American people decide through the election, and that in 1864, Congress was in a recess when Taney died and during the election, so even if Lincoln had nominated a replacement, they wouldn't have been able to be confirmed until December when the Senate was back.

The Federalist Society's analysis similarly noted Lincoln said no such thing; the fact is that the Senate in 1864 was out of session until December, which ruled out a pre-election confirmation, and added that Lincoln had his own political reasons for postponing his nomination until after the election, given the challenges of both the Civil War and his effort to win re-election, which required the support of a fragile coalition. clickondetroit's fact-check concluded similarly that while the history is right, the Senator's characterization isn't fully accurate — Lincoln did wait to announce his replacement until December, after winning reelection, but understandings of the time show Lincoln acted more out of political shrewdness to win the election rather than wanting the American people to vote first.

However, not all historians agreed with this "revisionist" framing — a Just Security piece co-authored by Lincoln biographer Harold Holzer pushed back, arguing the evidence abounds that Lincoln deferred his choice primarily because he understood how improper—even defiant—it would be to choose Taney's successor with only a few weeks left before voters went to the polls, and concluded Lincoln would have approved Kamala Harris' interpretations of one of his noblest, and riskiest, decisions when the chief justiceship became vacant in October 1864: deferring to the judgment of democracy. That was Lincoln's objective.

So the underlying facts Harris cited (timing of the vacancy, delay until after the election) were accurate, but the claim that Lincoln explicitly said this was to let voters decide is unsupported by direct evidence, and the more immediate practical reason was that the Senate was out of session — a key detail Harris omitted. This matches the headline's framing that the statement "misses key details," a conclusion echoed across nearly every mainstream fact-check outlet (Washington Post, USA Today's KING5/VERIFY affiliate, National Review, Fox News), even as some historians defended the substance of her interpretation.

However, full context shows Trump explicitly said he was not referring to neo-Nazis or white nationalists, whom he said 'should be condemned totally' — a caveat frequently omitted when the quote is used to imply Trump called white supremacists 'fine people,' which fact-checkers have flagged as an important nuance even while confirming the quote itself is real.

As for whether Trump actually said this, the record confirms he did use this phrase during an August 15, 2017 press conference about the Charlottesville "Unite the Right" rally. According to multiple contemporaneous transcripts, Trump stated: "TRUMP: ... you had some very bad people in that group, but you also had people that were very fine people, on both sides."

The transcript confirms Harris did say this at the October 7, 2020 vice presidential debate: "When asked about the Trump administration's response to COVID-19, Harris said, 'The president said it was a hoax.'"

However, multiple fact-checkers found this to be an inaccurate characterization of what Trump actually said. Trump's actual quote, from a February 28, 2020 rally, was calling Democratic criticism of his administration's response "their new hoax" — not the virus itself. As NBC News noted: "Harris misstates Trump's use of the term hoax, which Trump invoked when he said Democrats 'are politicizing the coronavirus.' Asked a day after his 'hoax' remark, Trump again said he was referring to Democrats' actions."

Similarly, widely-reported figures from the World Poverty Clock in 2018 found 86.9 million Nigerians living in extreme poverty, representing nearly 50% of its estimated 180 million population, and academic literature citing the same source put the figure at about 51% or 105 million of Nigeria's 205 million population.

It's worth noting that Nigeria's own National Bureau of Statistics, using a different (national, not international) poverty line, reported a lower figure: "In Nigeria 40.1 percent of total population were classified as poor. In other words, on average 4 out of 10 individuals in Nigeria has real per capita expenditures below 137,430 Naira per year." That NBS figure, however, measures overall poverty against Nigeria's national poverty line, not "extreme poverty" against the international line, so it isn't a direct contradiction of the 49% claim — it's simply a different metric.

Given that multiple independent, credible sources (World Bank projections, World Poverty Clock estimates) around 2019-2020 put Nigeria's extreme poverty rate using the international $1.90/day line in the high-40s to low-50s percent range, the 49% figure cited in the tweet falls squarely within the range of legitimate contemporaneous estimates.

claim: Wearing face masks leads to permanent neurological damage, especially in children.
justification: The claim traces to a viral transcript of Dr. Griesz-Brisson's video, which multiple fact-checkers (AFP, Africa Check, ScienceTimes) investigated and found unsupported. Independent medical experts (German Society for Neurology, German Society for Pneumology, Virginia Tech airborne-disease researcher) confirmed masks do not block oxygen or trap dangerous CO2 levels, and no evidence supports claims of permanent neurological damage from mask-wearing, especially not in children.

trace.raw_text:
Based on multiple independent sources, this claim has been thoroughly investigated and debunked by fact-checkers.

The claim originated from a viral Facebook/social media transcript (attributed to Henna Maria) of a video by German neurologist Dr. Margarite Griesz-Brisson, which asserted that masks cause oxygen deprivation, carbon dioxide buildup, and permanent, irreversible brain damage, particularly in children. The transcript claims that if you forget your phone number, brain breakdown began 20-30 years ago, and that mask-wearing amplifies degenerative processes through oxygen deprivation, with nerve cells unable to regenerate once lost.

However, AFP Fact Check directly investigated these claims with medical experts. Philipp Lepper, a member of the German Society for Pneumology and Respiratory Medicine, explained that since the amount of air behind the mask is very small and is mixed with fresh air each time you breathe in, this has no effect on oxygen and carbon dioxide levels measured in the body, because air flows freely through the mask. Regarding the specific claim about hippocampal nerve cells, the Secretary General of the German Society for Neurology confirmed nerve cells can't survive more than three minutes without oxygen, but said this cannot be triggered by wearing a mask, since masks do not cut off oxygen.

Other researchers corroborated this. Linsey Marr, a professor of civil and environmental engineering at Virginia Tech and expert in airborne disease transmission, noted that while masks can block particles, they do not block gases like oxygen and carbon dioxide, and a study of people wearing surgical masks while walking showed no noticeable increases in carbon dioxide or drops in blood oxygen. A separate fact-check by Africa Check found that even N95 masks have not been shown to cause oxygen deprivation or increased CO2 inhalation except in very rare cases with severe pre-existing health conditions, and a University of Maryland public health professor confirmed there was no increase in carbon dioxide intake from mask use. Additionally, experts denied that wearing a mask, even in infants, contributes to brain harm, noting that neurological complications seen in COVID-19 are predominately secondary effects of severe illness itself, not mask-wearing.

It's also worth noting that when AFP contacted Griesz-Brisson directly, she responded by email but did not answer the fact-checkers' questions, instead asking for respect for her work and experience. Separately, legitimate research on masks and children has found real but much more limited effects — such as on emotion-reading and speech perception — with no evidence of permanent neurological damage, and Psychology Today explicitly noted it is unlikely that masking will cause prosopagnosia, the neurological disorder characterized by an inability to distinguish faces.

claim: Tax avoidance costs £90 billion per year.
justification: The £90bn figure does circulate in UK political debate (cited in a 2020 Commons motion and originating from Richard Murphy's Tax Research UK estimate), but it refers to the entire 'tax gap' — combining evasion, error, non-payment, hidden economy and avoidance — not 'tax avoidance' alone. trace.raw_text:
Based on my research, this claim conflates two different concepts that are often mixed together in UK tax debates.

The £90 billion figure does exist in public discourse, but it does **not** refer specifically to "tax avoidance" — it refers to an alternative, broader estimate of the entire UK "tax gap" (which includes evasion, error, non-payment, criminal attacks, hidden economy activity, *and* avoidance combined). This figure originates largely from tax campaigner Richard Murphy/Tax Research UK, who added HMRC's admitted rate of non-payment and error to shadow-economy and legal-interpretation-dispute estimates to arrive at "£89.4 billion... Call it £90 billion for the sake of argument". This same £90bn upper-bound estimate was cited in a February 2020 House of Commons opposition day debate, where the motion noted that the tax gap "has been estimated at between a minimum of £35 billion and £90 billion", with MPs noting "other experts have suggested... the tax gap could be as high as £90 billion overall".

However, this £90bn is explicitly the **total tax gap**, not "tax avoidance" alone. Official HMRC figures, which break the tax gap down by taxpayer behaviour, show tax avoidance specifically is a much smaller sliver: it was estimated that in 2019/20 the financial loss from tax avoidance was £1.5 billion, while the cost of tax evasion was £5.5 billion, and HMRC's official overall tax gap for that period was £35 billion for 2019/20, representing 5.3% of total tax liabilities. More recent HMRC data confirms avoidance remains a small fraction: the avoidance tax gap is estimated to be £0.8 billion in 2024 to 2025... Avoidance is the smallest proportion of the tax gap at 1%.

So the claim takes a disputed, campaigner-derived upper-bound estimate of the *entire* tax gap (evasion + avoidance + error + non-payment + hidden economy) and mislabels it as the cost of "tax avoidance" specifically — a much narrower category that official estimates put at roughly £1-2 billion a year, not £90 billion.

I found no specific record of "Heather Young" or her exact Facebook post, but I have substantial evidence on the underlying medical claim about flu shot safety, which is what matters most here.

Based on CDC and other medical sources, flu shots have an excellent safety record. Most side effects are mild: many people who get an annual flu vaccine report no side effects at all, and most side effects reported after flu vaccination are mild and disappear on their own in a few days without treatment. While severe reactions are theoretically possible, they are extremely rare: findings from vaccine safety monitoring systems and scientific studies have shown that flu vaccines have an excellent safety profile, and hundreds of millions of Americans have safely received flu vaccines for more than 50 years, with the body of scientific evidence overwhelmingly supporting their safety.

Regarding Guillain-Barré syndrome, one of the most cited "severe" risks: the data on an association between seasonal inactivated influenza vaccine and GBS varies from season to season, and when there has been an increased risk, it has been in the range of 1-2 additional GBS cases per million flu vaccine doses administered, with a person more likely to get GBS after flu disease than after getting a flu vaccine. Similarly, life-threatening allergic reactions are rare: life threatening allergic reactions to the flu shot are rare.

claim: In England You can get a £3,000 fine for not wearing a cloth over your face at the time of this claim.
justification: A first-time offence for not wearing a face covering in England carried a fine of only £100-£200, not £3,000; the higher figure only applied as a maximum ceiling reached after multiple repeat violations under a doubling ('laddering') penalty system. Moreover, by the claim's date (30 Sept 2020), regulations effective 23-24 September had already raised that maximum to £6,400, making even the £3,000 figure outdated.

trace.raw_text:
Based on the evidence, this claim is misleading because it drastically overstates what a first-time offender would face and conflates a maximum "ceiling" penalty with a routine fine.

The actual penalty structure in England for not wearing a face covering was tiered ("laddered"), not a flat fine. In August 2020, regulations set the original face coverings regulations stipulated that a penalty notice of £100 could be issued to someone over the age of 18 who was in breach of those regulations and that that would be halved to £50 if paid within 14 days. Only for repeat offenders did the fine escalate: for each additional breach of the face covering regulations on public transport and in relevant places, the fixed penalty notice amount now doubles, up to a maximum of £3,200—a system that is now known as laddering.

Critically, by the date this claim was made (30 September 2020), the rules had already changed again. New regulations that took effect on 23–24 September 2020 amend both the original regulations to increase the applicable penalties under them. They increase the fine for a first offence from £100 to £200 (in both cases, halved if paid within 14 days). The penalty will still double for each subsequent offence, with the maximum increasing to £6,400. This is corroborated by a separate source noting that the Health Protection (Coronavirus, Wearing of Face Coverings in a Relevant Place and on Public Transport) (England) (Amendment) (No. 3) Regulations 2020 (SI 2020/1026) doubled the penalties for breach to a minimum of £200 (£100 if paid within 14 days), with the ladder maxing out well above £3,000.

So at the time the claim was made, the true maximum penalty was £6,400, not £3,000 — and even that figure only applied to someone with multiple repeat violations, not a single instance of not wearing a face covering. A first-time offender faced a fine of just £100–£200. Presenting "£3,000" as the fine one "can get" for simply not wearing a mask omits this crucial tiered structure and uses an outdated, and much lower, maximum figure.

justification: Biden did say the words 'dregs of society' in a 2018 speech, but multiple fact-checks (USA Today, Reuters) found he was referring to a small group of virulent extremists (alt-right, KKK) who oppose LGBTQ rights, not to Trump supporters generally. Biden did use the phrase "dregs of society" during a September 2018 speech at the Human Rights Campaign dinner, but fact-checkers found the context was distorted when Trump-aligned sources (and later the Trump 2020 campaign in an October 2020 video) claimed it referred to all Trump supporters.

In the actual speech, Biden was discussing violence against the LGBTQ community and how "forces of intolerance remain determined to undermine and roll back the progress" many have made, mentioning that those who want to take away LGBTQ rights — like members of the alt-right and the KKK — have an ally in President Trump. Crucially, Biden never specifically said that all of Trump's supporters fell into that category.

claim: A Supreme Court nominee has never been nominated and installed while a presidential election is already underway.
justification: Historical records show multiple Supreme Court nominees were both nominated and confirmed during presidential election years while campaigns were underway, including Melville Fuller (1888), Mahlon Pitney (1912), Louis Brandeis (1916), Benjamin Cardozo (1932), and Frank Murphy (1940). Scholarly and journalistic sources from the time explicitly note there is no historical practice of avoiding nomination/confirmation in election years. A narrower claim (no nominee confirmed within weeks of Election Day itself) had more support, but the broad claim as stated is false.

trace.raw_text:
Based on my research, this claim is contradicted by well-documented historical precedent.

Multiple Supreme Court justices have been nominated *and* confirmed while a presidential election campaign was already underway, well before Election Day, in several election years:

- In 1888, Supreme Court Justice Morrison R. Waite died within seven months of election day, leaving President Grover Cleveland, a Democrat, to fill the spot, and the Republican Party's slim majority allowed for the confirmation of President Cleveland's nominee, Melville Weston Fuller, who went on to serve on the Court for over twenty years as Chief Justice — notably under divided government.
- In 1912, President William Taft nominated Mahlon Pitney to succeed John Marshall Harlan, and the Republican-controlled Senate confirmed Pitney on March 18, 1912.
- In 1916, President Woodrow Wilson nominated Louis Brandeis, and the Democratic-controlled Senate confirmed Justice Brandeis on June 1, 1916 — months before the November election.
- In 1932, President Herbert Hoover nominated Benjamin Cardozo, and a Republican-controlled Senate confirmed Justice Cardozo on February 24, 1932.
- In 1940, President Franklin Roosevelt nominated Frank Murphy, and a Democratic-controlled Senate confirmed Justice Murphy on January 16, 1940.

Election-law scholarship on this period concludes plainly: the historical record does not reveal any instances since at least 1900 of the president failing to nominate and/or the Senate failing to confirm a nominee in a presidential election year because of the impending election, and there were several nominations and confirmations of Justices during presidential election years.

Notably, even Trump's campaign directly rebutted this type of claim from Biden at the time, stating Joe Biden is falsely claiming there is no precedent to confirm a Supreme Court justice in an election year, when there have been 29 prior vacancies during election years or a lame-duck period and in all cases, the president nominated a justice.

There is a narrower, more defensible version of the argument Democrats made in 2020 — that no nominee had previously been confirmed so close to Election Day itself (within weeks), as Senate staff noted materials from the offices of the Secretary of the Senate do not show such a precedent for a confirmation between July and Election Day. But the broad claim that a nominee has "never" been nominated and installed while an election is underway is false — it happened repeatedly, including with nominees confirmed months before Election Day in 1888, 1912, 1916, 1932, and 1940.

The claim asserts that COVID-19 death benefits can be claimed under **both** PMJJBY and PMSBY schemes. Fact-checks from the same period (September 2020) show this is only partially accurate.

claim: US President Donald Trump's executive order on September 24, 2020 legally ensures health coverage protections for those with pre existing medical conditions.
justification: Contemporaneous reporting from CNBC, NBC News, KFF Health News, and legal scholars consistently found the order merely declared a policy statement with no enforcement mechanism or legal teeth, not a binding legal guarantee. Legal experts explicitly said it had 'no more legal weight than a campaign slogan,' and even HHS Secretary Azar called it a 'request' rather than a law, while the actual enforceable pre-existing conditions protections came from the ACA, which the Trump administration was simultaneously suing to overturn.

trace.raw_text:
Based on multiple contemporaneous reports from CNBC, NBC News, US News, KFF Health News, and others, the evidence strongly contradicts the claim that this executive order "legally ensures" health coverage protections for pre-existing conditions.

The order itself was largely a statement of policy intent rather than a binding legal mandate. President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Sept. 24 that says that people with preexisting conditions can get affordable insurance, but it doesn't explain how. The actual text was vague: "It has been and will continue to be the policy of the United States to give Americans seeking healthcare more choice, lower costs, and better care and to ensure that Americans with pre-existing conditions can obtain the insurance of their choice at affordable rates."

Legal experts were emphatic that this order carried no binding force. Nicholas Bagley, a University of Michigan law professor, said unless "Congress has adopted a law prohibiting discrimination against the sick, or President Trump is exercising authority that Congress has delegated to him, his executive orders don't have legal effect." "They have no more legal weight than a campaign slogan — and that's all this executive order is," he said. Similarly, a University of Pennsylvania law professor noted "were the court to hold the Affordable Care Act unconstitutional, the executive order would still do nothing, because it has no enforcement power."

Even HHS Secretary Alex Azar acknowledged the order's limited nature, telling a reporter that these executive orders are not laws, but act as requests. KFF's health policy chief Larry Levitt bluntly described it as "a pinky promise to protect people with preexisting conditions."

Importantly, the pre-existing protections already legally in place came from the Affordable Care Act, not this order. As the American Public Health Association noted, "It isn't policy. It's the law. One of the triumphs of the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare, is the provision making it illegal to deny coverage to people with preexisting medical conditions." Meanwhile, the new Trump executive order is not enforceable, but the ACA is. This is especially ironic given that the Trump administration attempts to repeal Obamacare, which has a provision that prevents insurers from discriminating against Americans with preexisting medical conditions.

claim: A mail-in ballot application for voting in the US presidential election which was sent to a deceased grandfather in the State of New Mexico is evidence of potential widespread voter fraud via mail-in ballots.
justification: While an isolated mail ballot application being sent to a deceased person is a real and common occurrence, fact-checkers and election officials consistently attribute this to outdated mailing databases/clerical errors rather than evidence of fraud, and New Mexico has specific safeguards (obituary checks, Vital Statistics reports, ERIC data-matching) designed to prevent such applications from resulting in an actual counted fraudulent vote. Framing a single such anecdote as evidence of 'potential widespread voter fraud' goes well beyond what the underlying fact supports, echoing a pattern of similar viral claims in 2020 that were repeatedly debunked.

trace.raw_text:
Based on my research, I was unable to find the specific original Facebook post by "Don Larkin" from September 25, 2020, but I found extensive, directly relevant fact-checking on this exact category of claim (a mail ballot application arriving addressed to a deceased person as "evidence" of fraud), which was a very common viral claim pattern in 2020.

**What the evidence shows:**

1. **Receiving an application ≠ fraud, and is a well-documented, non-fraudulent occurrence.** Voter list/mailing databases used by campaigns, county clerks, or third-party groups are frequently not updated in real time. A PolitiFact fact-check of a nearly identical claim (a mail ballot form addressed to a deceased mother in Texas) found "Sometimes databases used by campaign vendors or nonprofits to send mail are not up to date or accurate, resulting in a mail ballot application being sent to someone who died — or even to a dead pet." That same fact-check noted there is no evidence that campaigns or activists are submitting application forms on behalf of dead voters, and election officials track internally why an application is denied and states have policies to pursue cases of fraudulent registrations.

2. **New Mexico specifically has safeguards against this becoming actual fraud.** New Mexico's Secretary of State's office notes that during the voter list maintenance process New Mexico's election administrators, as required by law, must maintain and update their voter rolls continually — everything from checking obituaries, receiving monthly reports from NM Vital Statistics about deceased individuals, and suspending or reinstating voters based on conviction notices from the Department of Corrections. The state also participates in the Electronic Registration Information Center (ERIC), which uses information from motor vehicle departments, Social Security Administration records, and other databases to compare voters across all member states, resulting in New Mexico having some of the "cleanest" voter records in the United States.

3. **This general "dead voter" narrative has been repeatedly investigated and debunked at scale.** A 2014 GAO literature review found that in one state's examination of about 200 questioned "dead voter" cases from a 2010 election, all but 5 of the questioned votes could be attributed to errors by state or local officials—including clerical errors, data matching errors, errors in scanning voter registration forms, and the issuance of absentee ballots in the wrong name—or to applications for absentee ballots by voters who died before the election. Similarly, a 2007 investigation of about 100 "dead voters" in Missouri revealed that every single purported case was properly attributed either to a matching error, a problem in the underlying data, or a clerical error by elections officials or voters.

4. **No widespread fraud was found in the 2020 election overall.** Election officials nationwide, including in New Mexico, have stated the 2020 election was the "most secure in history," according to election officials across the country, and no evidence of widespread voter fraud was ever proven in any state.

**Assessment:** A single mail ballot *application* reaching a deceased person's address is a real, recurring, and well-understood phenomenon caused by outdated mailing/voter-file data — not an indicator of an actual fraudulent vote, let alone "widespread" fraud. Even if the underlying anecdote (an application sent to a deceased grandfather) is true, using it as evidence of "potential widespread voter fraud" mischaracterizes what fact-checkers and election officials have consistently found: such incidents are almost always clerical/database errors that are typically caught before any fraudulent ballot could be cast and counted.

Multiple contemporaneous Philippine news reports confirm the actual budget figures for the Office of the Vice President (OVP) under Leni Robredo for 2021. A Senate panel restored around P45 million to the Office of the Vice President's proposed budget for 2021 after it was cut by the Department of Budget and Management, with the OVP having requested P723 million pesos for next year. The final figure came in even higher: Vice President Leni Robredo's office got a P229-million increase, as reflected in the 2021 General Appropriations Bill ratified by Congress, placing her official budget for next year at P900 million.

claim: Transitioning to 100 per cent renewable electricity generation increase power prices in New Zealand

Independent fact-checkers (AAP FactCheck via Newshub) rated the claim 'mostly false' because experts, including an ICCC member, said the actual pumped-hydro option was expected to lower prices in the longer term, contradicting the blanket claim that transitioning to 100% renewables would increase prices.

The claim stems from a specific statement Judith Collins made during a September 22, 2020 TVNZ leaders' debate, where she said transitioning to 100% renewable electricity would increase power prices, citing "the experts" predicting a 14% increase for residential users.

Fact-checkers found this claim to have real substance but with important context missing. Collins' office referred to a report by the Interim Climate Change Committee (ICCC), which commissioned a model to look at the economic impact of meeting the target, finding retail electricity prices could increase by 14 percent for residential users, 29 percent for commercial users and 39 percent for industrial users. This confirms the 14% figure Collins cited was accurate and did come from government-commissioned expert modelling.

However, crucial context was omitted: this model was based on achieving 100 percent renewable electricity by "overbuilding" renewable generation and adding batteries to make up for years when hydro dams were low — not the pumped hydro scheme the government was actually pursuing. A spokesperson for Ardern said the pumped hydro scheme would be significantly cheaper than the options the ICCC investigated and would lower electricity prices for both consumers and businesses "in the longer term." Additionally, Dr Keith Turner, one of six experts on the ICCC and former CEO of Meridian Energy, said the Lake Onslow scheme could lead to lower electricity prices, noting the $4 billion cost could increase prices by 0.5 to 0.75 cents per kilowatt hour, but savings would likely offset that.

This directly matches Newshub/AAP FactCheck's own conclusion, which rated the claim as "mostly false" — Collins cited real modelling numbers, but applied them to the wrong policy (the ICCC's "overbuild" scenario rather than the actual pumped-hydro plan the government was pursuing), creating a misleading impression about the specific policy under discussion.

It is caused by various species of the genus Brucella, from which, B. abortus, B. melitensis, and B. suis are the most important ones with respect to their zoonotic potential. Several thousand people in northwest China tested positive for a bacterial disease, in an outbreak caused by a leak at a biopharmaceutical company, and the Health Commission of Lanzhou confirmed that 3,245 people had contracted brucellosis, which is often caused by contact with livestock carrying the bacteria brucella. This was traced to a factory leak, not a new virus: Chinese authorities said thousands of people in northwest China tested positive for a bacterial infection after an outbreak in 2019, stemming from a factory leak at a biopharmaceutical company.

So the claim conflates a real 2020 news story (a bacterial contamination incident at a Chinese vaccine factory) with the false assertion that brucellosis itself is a "new virus." Based on the evidence gathered, this claim contains multiple factual errors and misrepresents well-established history.

**On authorship:** The claim that Amelia (Aemilia) Bassano wrote Shakespeare's plays is a fringe theory, not established fact. The Emilia Lanier theory of Shakespeare authorship contends that Lanier is the actual author of at least part of the plays and poems attributed to William Shakespeare, but as is the case with dozens of other candidates, this idea is not accepted by the large majority of Shakespeare scholars. The theory originated with John Hudson, scholar and theatre producer, who in 2008 introduced the idea that Lanier wrote the works of Shakespeare, and academic critics have called it implausible; one professor stated "The idea that she was known to all these people and that some elaborate conspiracy of virtually everyone of significance in London in the 17th century would 'cover-up' her supposed authorship of Shakespeare's plays is ridiculous."

Historians have never described Amelia as being of African ancestry, though some agree she may have been dark-complected, which is why she is sometimes referred to as "Shakespeare's Dark Lady." Fact-checking outlets have explicitly rejected this framing: Fact-checkers like USA Today, Africa Check and AAP all reach the same conclusion: there is no evidence that a black woman or Aemilia Bassano wrote Shakespeare's plays.

**On being unpublished:** This is the most clearly false part of the claim. Bassano (as Aemilia Lanyer) actually published a book of poetry in her lifetime — her 1611 volume Salve Deus Rex Judaeorum has been seen as protofeminist, and she has a claim to be one of the first women poets with a substantial body of commercially-published work in the English language. In fact, she was the first Englishwoman to assert herself as a professional poet through her single volume of poems, Salve Deus Rex Judaeorum (1611). claim: The UK public won’t be able to claim compensation if unlicensed vaccines damage our health.
justification: While there was a legitimate concern in September 2020 about compensation for emergency-authorised 'unlicensed' COVID vaccines, the UK government specifically extended the Vaccine Damage Payment Scheme to cover COVID-19 vaccinations (including those under emergency use authorisation) via a Statutory Instrument effective 31 December 2020, before any mass public rollout occurred. Additional legal routes such as product liability and clinical negligence claims also remained available, contradicting the blanket claim that the public would have no compensation route.

trace.raw_text:
Based on my research, I can now assess this claim.

The claim was made on 13 September 2020 — at a time when no COVID-19 vaccine had yet been authorised in the UK and there was public debate about whether pharmaceutical companies' liability exemptions would leave vaccinated people without recourse if harmed. Elnaugh's own "Letter to your MP" from this period explicitly asked "Please confirm whether the Government will compensate individuals and their families should illness/death result from these vaccinations?", reflecting the underlying concern behind the claim.

However, the UK has a long-standing no-fault compensation mechanism, the Vaccine Damage Payment Scheme (VDPS), which was created in 1979 to provide significant payment to people who are severely disabled as a result of vaccinations against certain diseases, and it is not necessary to demonstrate negligence in order to qualify. Crucially, the government moved specifically to close the gap the claim warns about: the government is taking this precautionary step in advance of a rollout of an authorised COVID-19 vaccine, and in the very rare possibility where someone is severely disabled as a result of taking a COVID-19 vaccine, they can access financial assistance through the Vaccine Damage Payments Scheme. This was formalised in law: Article 2 of this Order adds COVID-19 to the diseases to which the Vaccine Damage Payments Act 1979 applies, effective from 31 December 2020, pursuant to the Vaccine Damage Payments (Specified Disease) Order 2020 — i.e., before the mass rollout to the public. Analysis of the scheme also confirms that this coverage extends to vaccines used under emergency/temporary authorisations, not just fully licensed ones: The UK NFCS covers vaccines for specified diseases listed in Section 1(2) of the Act or added by a Statutory Instrument which are administered in the UK. It includes vaccines approved for emergency use and standard approvals.

Beyond the VDPS, additional legal routes existed: individuals may also have a claim for clinical negligence against their healthcare provider if they believe they did not provide informed consent when receiving the vaccine, and separately product liability claims confer strict liability on the defendant, meaning the claimant is not required to prove any fault or negligence on behalf of the manufacturer, though this can be limited by a development-risk defence.

So, while there was a legitimate concern in September 2020 (before any authorisation, and before the scheme was formally extended) about whether compensation would be available for emergency-authorised/"unlicensed" COVID vaccines, the government acted specifically to guarantee that coverage before any public rollout occurred, and multiple compensation/legal avenues (VDPS, product liability, clinical negligence) existed once vaccination began. As a blanket claim that the UK public "won't be able to claim compensation," this does not hold up against what actually happened.

claim: Western Wildfires Are evidence Of A Coordinated Antifa Campaign To 'Burn The Country Down
justification: The claim that antifa was conducting a 'coordinated campaign' to burn the country down via the 2020 Western wildfires was investigated and explicitly debunked by the FBI's Portland field office and multiple county sheriff's offices in Oregon, which found the specific antifa-arson rumors 'untrue.' Reporting also traced the rumor's spread partly to Russian state media and found no evidence of any organized arson campaign by antifa; Facebook subsequently removed posts spreading this claim.

trace.raw_text:
The search results provide extensive, consistent evidence on this claim. This is a well-documented case from September 2020.

The FBI's Portland field office directly investigated and rejected these claims. "FBI Portland and local law enforcement agencies have been receiving reports that extremists are responsible for setting wildfires in Oregon. With our state and local partners, the FBI has investigated several such reports and found them to be untrue," the FBI Portland Division said in a statement.

Multiple local law enforcement agencies across Oregon separately debunked the specific rumors circulating at the time. The Douglas County Sheriff's Office in Southern Oregon took to Facebook to knock down rumors about six antifa members being arrested for setting fires, stating "THIS IS NOT TRUE! Unfortunately, people are spreading this rumor and it is causing problems." Similarly, the Medford Police Department posted saying "This is a made up graphic and story. We did not arrest this person for arson, nor anyone affiliated with Antifa or 'Proud Boys'... Also, no confirmed gatherings of Antifa which has also been reported."

Reporting also traced the origin of the rumor to misinformation rather than verified facts. The blazes consuming the West Coast became part of an election cycle culture war when claims that antifa started wildfires in Portland went viral, but there's no evidence that antifa started any wildfires, though conservatives on social media ran with the claim anyway. Investigators found the theory traced back partly to Russian state media amplification: its first big boost appears to have come from RT, in the form of an article that smashed together separate pieces of information about policing in Portland and the wildfires, insinuating a nefarious and non-existent link between the two.

Facebook itself took action against these claims. Facebook said it would take down erroneous posts claiming anti-fascist activists have been maliciously sparking wildfires in Oregon and other Western states, noting there is no evidence Oregon's fires were caused by arson from far-left activists, and removing false claims that the wildfires were started by certain groups.

Law enforcement's overall conclusion at the time was unambiguous: there's no evidence antifa or any other political group is committing arson at this time, and online speculation wastes precious resources needed to save lives.

This claim fits squarely into the pattern of "antifa wildfire" misinformation that spread virally on Facebook in September 2020 and was specifically and repeatedly debunked by the FBI, multiple county sheriff's offices, and Facebook itself.
